A hash checks integrity relative to a trusted expected value; it does not make an attacker-provided model and attacker-provided hash safe. The longer-lived service project uses a bounded JSON model representation to avoid arbitrary object deserialization at that serving boundary.
key_terms: Model artifact
A serialized bundle of fitted state together with its interface contract: feature order, units, preprocessing and dependencies.
Artifact integrity
Agreement between an artifact's SHA256 digest and a trusted expected value. It detects changed bytes but does not make an untrusted file safe.
Model registry
The MLflow store of named models whose numbered versions each link to a logged artifact and its run.
Alias
A movable name such as candidate that points to one registered model version. Setting it does not accept or deploy the model.
Trusted serialization
Loading joblib or pickle files only from a trusted source, because deserializing Python objects can execute arbitrary code.
units.syntax: joblib writes and reads the program's own trusted fitted pipeline. A manifest retains feature order and SHA256. MLflow create_model_version links the artifact to its run, while set_registered_model_alias and get_model_version_by_alias exercise actual version resolution. A candidate alias is a label, not automatic acceptance or deployment.

worked.title: Verify a trusted artifact and registry link
worked.explanation: The first program checks bytes before reloading its own model, compares prediction parity and registers the artifact with MLflow. It verifies that the alias resolves to the expected version and run.
worked.expected: Reloaded predictions match, and the actual registry version retains its linked run.

worked.title: Detect integrity and semantic changes
worked.explanation: The second case changes an artifact payload and a unit definition separately. The same feature names do not make hours and minutes compatible. Both exact-byte identity and semantic contract versioning are therefore needed.
worked.expected: Tampered bytes fail their expected hash and the changed unit contract has a different identity.

exercises.title: Record feature order
exercises.task: Keep the input field sequence with the artifact.
exercises.check: A consumer can reconstruct the expected interface.
exercises.hint: An unlabeled array is ambiguous.
exercises.answer: Validate names, order and transformations before inference. A column permutation can change predictions without producing a type error.

exercises.title: Test a byte change
exercises.task: Modify the saved model after recording its hash.
exercises.check: Integrity verification rejects the changed bytes.
exercises.hint: Check before deserialization.
exercises.answer: Retain a trusted expected identity and fail clearly on mismatch. Do not merely recompute and overwrite the expected hash.

exercises.title: Reject untrusted loading
exercises.task: Explain why a matching attacker-supplied hash is insufficient.
exercises.check: It does not establish authenticity or safe code.
exercises.hint: Integrity and trust are different properties.
exercises.answer: Use an appropriate trusted publication mechanism and safe supported model formats. Never load arbitrary remote pickle/joblib content as a convenience.

exercises.title: Inspect registry resolution
exercises.task: Read the version behind the candidate alias.
exercises.check: It matches the intended registered artifact and run.
exercises.hint: Aliases can move.
exercises.answer: Record the resolved version used for a decision. A mutable label alone is not a complete provenance record.

exercises.title: Change the feature meaning
exercises.task: Convert usage hours to minutes without adapting the model.
exercises.check: The contract marks the incompatibility.
exercises.hint: Types and names can remain unchanged.
exercises.answer: Version the feature interface and evaluate a compatible model. Do not silently retarget an old artifact to changed units.

exercises.title: Define promotion evidence
exercises.task: List checks needed before moving an accepted serving alias.
exercises.check: It includes compatibility, quality, operational and rollback evidence.
exercises.hint: Registry storage is not the decision.
exercises.answer: Keep the actual acceptance policy and responsible review with the version. The later rollout and service project demonstrate controlled activation separately.

units.diagnosis: A model can deserialize successfully and still expect the wrong inputs. An alias can resolve correctly and still point to an unaccepted candidate. Inspect artifact identity, feature meaning and acceptance evidence separately, and reject untrusted executable serialization.
units.transfer: Verify real registry linkage and prediction parity while keeping integrity, authenticity and deployment acceptance distinct. Prefer a safe bounded representation at a local demonstration service boundary.
units.lab: Publish and resolve a model artifact with an explicit trusted interface. Run both complete local examples, explain the changed assumption, and retain evidence for the six practice changes.

units.title: A real HTTP contract before a network deployment
units.outcome: Define and test a serving contract with positive and negative requests.
units.theory:
A serving interface should define which inputs it accepts and what evidence it returns. Validation errors are part of that interface, not an incidental exception path. The model version and feature contract should be visible so a prediction can be interpreted and compared with its source artifact.

This lesson exercises an actual FastAPI application through an in-process ASGI client. It tests HTTP parsing, schema validation, route execution and response encoding without starting a network server. The first case compares the route's probability with the same model's direct prediction. The second rejects a negative usage value and an undeclared target field.

These checks do not establish DNS, sockets, container networking, load capacity or external authentication. The complete local-system project later starts a real loopback HTTP service and qualifies those declared lifecycle paths separately. Keeping the evidence layers distinct prevents a useful unit-level API test from being mislabeled as a deployed system.
key_terms: ASGI
The Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface, the Python standard through which a server passes HTTP requests to an application such as FastAPI.
Request schema
A Pydantic model declaring accepted fields, bounds and allowed values. With extra fields forbidden, an undeclared target field is rejected.
Validation error
The structured HTTP 422 response FastAPI returns when a request violates the schema; it is part of the interface, not an incidental failure.
TestClient
A client that sends real ASGI requests to the application inside the process, covering parsing, validation and routing without opening a socket.
Model version
The identifier returned with each prediction so the response can be traced to its source artifact and feature contract.
units.syntax: The Pydantic request model declares bounded usage/tickets and an allowed region vocabulary, with extra fields forbidden. A POST route converts the validated object into the model's expected frame and returns a numeric probability plus version. TestClient sends real ASGI requests inside the process. The networked project uses the same contract principles with Docker-owned state and loopback publication.

worked.title: Compare HTTP-contract and direct inference
worked.explanation: The first case submits a valid JSON body through the application. It checks status 200, the version label and numeric agreement with direct model inference. That makes the route behavior observable.
worked.expected: The accepted request returns a probability matching the fitted model and version fixture-v1.

worked.title: Reject invalid and undeclared input
worked.explanation: The second case sends a negative value and a label field that is not part of the prediction interface. Both must be rejected before model execution under the declared schema.
worked.expected: Both requests return 422 validation responses.

exercises.title: Test a boundary value
exercises.task: Submit usage 0 and the declared maximum.
exercises.check: The response follows the documented bounds.
exercises.hint: Boundaries need explicit tests.
exercises.answer:
Check both accepted boundaries and values immediately outside them. Do not infer request validation from the model's numerical output.

The Request model declares usage with ge=0 and le=10000, so usage 0 and usage 10000 should both return 200, while -0.01 and 10000.01 should return 422. The same holds for tickets at 0 and 100 versus 101. Seeing a sensible probability for a value is no proof it was inside the contract: the logistic model would score usage 50000 without complaint.

exercises.title: Reject a hidden target
exercises.task: Add label to an otherwise valid request.
exercises.check: The API rejects the undeclared field.
exercises.hint: The serving contract is an allowlist.
exercises.answer:
Extra-field rejection helps catch client mistakes and accidental leakage. It does not replace broader data and access controls.

Example_two already posts label 1 and gets 422 because of extra="forbid". Remove that line from model_config and pydantic's default is to ignore unknown fields, so the same request returns 200 and the client never learns it was sending its target. Assert the status code, not just that a probability came back.

exercises.title: Inspect the model version
exercises.task: Keep the returned version with a prediction record.
exercises.check: The observation identifies its model.
exercises.hint: A score without version context is hard to reproduce.
exercises.answer:
Bind the version to the accepted artifact and feature contract. A display label should not diverge from the actual loaded state.

Notice that "fixture-v1" is a literal string in predict(), not a value read from the fitted pipeline. Refitting with a different training cutoff would still answer fixture-v1. Store the version on the loaded bundle and return that attribute, then verify two different fits produce two different versions.

exercises.title: Test categorical policy
exercises.task: Submit an unknown region.
exercises.check: It is rejected under this interface contract.
exercises.hint: The API may be stricter than an internal encoder.
exercises.answer:
Document that choice and ensure clients know the accepted vocabulary. A hidden fallback can create train/serve inconsistency.

region is Literal["north", "south"], so "east" returns 422 at the HTTP layer even though the pipeline underneath uses OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") and would have scored it as all zeros. The API contract is stricter than the model; send "east" through both paths to see 422 versus a probability.

exercises.title: Separate test boundaries
exercises.task: List what the in-process client has not tested.
exercises.check: It has not tested real network/container lifecycle.
exercises.hint: ASGI behavior is one evidence layer.
exercises.answer: Use the owned local-system checker for actual HTTP, startup, monitoring, rollback and replacement. Do not claim an external deployment from this unit alone.

exercises.title: Preserve safe errors
exercises.task: Describe a diagnostic that avoids exposing credentials or internals.
exercises.check: It is actionable without unnecessary sensitive detail.
exercises.hint: Error handling is part of the API.
exercises.answer:
Return a bounded public error and retain appropriate owned operational evidence. Do not echo arbitrary secrets or expose an administrative mutation route casually.

Recent FastAPI versions include each offending input in the 422 detail. If a client sent a token in an undeclared field, the error body could echo it back into a log. Return the field name and constraint, such as "usage must be <= 10000", and keep the full request only in owned, access-controlled evidence.

units.diagnosis: An HTTP 422 can be correct input rejection rather than a model failure. A 200 response can still carry the wrong model or transformation. Compare the route with direct inference, inspect the version and keep the limits of in-process testing explicit.
units.transfer: Verify model parity and version identity, then use the separate real Docker service project to qualify network and persistence behavior.
units.lab: Define and test a serving contract with positive and negative requests. Run both complete local examples, explain the changed assumption, and retain evidence for the six practice changes.

units.title: Orchestration, checkpoints and safe retries
units.outcome: Define checkpoint and retry behavior using artifact identities.
units.theory:
A workflow coordinator decides which stages can run, what evidence is complete and what should happen after interruption. Repeating a command is not automatically a safe retry. An operation may already have written an artifact before its response was lost, and a changed input may make an old checkpoint invalid.

The local example uses an explicit ledger to expose these mechanisms. It records the input identity, derived features, model state and publication identity. A deliberate interruption occurs after the feature checkpoint. Resuming with the same input reuses that completed stage and reaches the same publication identity on another run.

The second case changes the input and invalidates the prior derived state. This is a small Python workflow model, not a disguised Prefect deployment. The existing Python orchestration lessons introduce actual framework execution. The purpose here is to make the state and retry contract explicit before choosing a scheduler or distributing work.
key_terms: DAG
A directed acyclic graph of workflow stages in which each stage runs only after its predecessors have completed.
Checkpoint
A recorded completed artifact in the ledger that a resumed run reuses instead of recomputing.
Idempotency
The property that repeating an operation with the same input yields the same result, such as the same publication identity, without duplicate effects.
Input identity
A stable digest of the input data that ties derived artifacts to their source; a changed digest invalidates prior derived state.
Safe retry
Repeating a stage only when recorded evidence and input identity show that repetition cannot create a conflicting or duplicate result.
units.syntax: The ledger keys represent completed artifacts. A stable input digest identifies which data those artifacts belong to. Publication is created only after model state exists, and repeat execution with the same input returns the same identity. An input change clears derived state under this simple policy; a larger system may invalidate only affected descendants.

worked.title: Resume after a known interruption
worked.explanation: The first case fails deliberately after features are recorded. It confirms that publication is absent, then resumes and repeats the same run. The unchanged publication identity is evidence of the fixture's idempotent behavior.
worked.expected: The feature checkpoint survives; resumed model mean is 4 and repeated publication identity is unchanged.

worked.title: Invalidate work derived from changed input
worked.explanation: The second case changes one source value. Its digest, derived features, model mean and publication identity change. Reusing the old result would violate the dependency contract.
worked.expected: New features are [2, 4, 8] and the mean is 14/3.

exercises.title: Name the side effect
exercises.task: Identify which stage creates the consumer-facing result.
exercises.check: Publication is separate from feature and model computation.
exercises.hint: Retry risk depends on the operation.
exercises.answer:
Describe whether each stage is pure, idempotent or requires reconciliation. A successful earlier stage does not authorize all later effects.

In execute_pipeline the publication key holds digest(ledger["model"]); it is the only value a consumer reads. features and model are pure functions of events, so recomputing them is harmless, but publishing twice to a real destination would not be.

exercises.title: Add an uncertain outcome
exercises.task: Describe a timeout after publication may already have occurred.
exercises.check: The response checks the intended identity before repeating.
exercises.hint: Unknown differs from confirmed failure.
exercises.answer:
Read the publication record or artifact and determine whether the operation completed. Do not blindly repeat a non-idempotent effect.

Suppose the step after ledger["publication"] is assigned times out. Compare the stored publication with digest(ledger["model"]); if they match, the effect already happened and repeating it is unnecessary. Retrying unconditionally would be safe in this dictionary but could send a second notification in a real system.

exercises.title: Version the code
exercises.task: Include transformation-code identity with the input identity.
exercises.check: Changed logic invalidates incompatible reuse.
exercises.hint: Equal data does not imply equal computation.
exercises.answer:
Record the source or transformation version that produced a checkpoint. Reusing it under different logic can silently return stale results.

Change the transformation to 3 * x but keep events [1, 2, 3]. source_id is unchanged, so the ledger keeps features [2, 4, 6] and mean 4: a stale result with no error. Including a transform version in the digested identity, for example digest({"events": events, "transform": "double-v1"}), forces recomputation. Verify the new mean is 6.

exercises.title: Invalidate a descendant
exercises.task: Change a feature transformation and identify affected stages.
exercises.check: Model, evaluation and publication need new evidence.
exercises.hint: The artifact graph defines propagation.
exercises.answer:
Recompute the affected descendants or use a proven compatible reuse rule. A checkpoint is useful only with its dependencies.

Example_two shows the input case: [1, 2, 4] clears the whole ledger and yields features [2, 4, 8] and mean 14/3. Deleting only ledger["features"] after a code change would recompute features but keep the old model and publication, because those keys remain present.

exercises.title: Keep failure evidence
exercises.task: Retain the interruption reason and completed stages.
exercises.check: The next attempt can explain what was reused.
exercises.hint: A retry count alone is incomplete.
exercises.answer:
Record stage identities and actual outcomes. Avoid overwriting the original failure with a later success without preserving the distinction.

After the deliberate interruption the ledger holds only source_id and features, with no record that a failure occurred. Add an attempts list with the RuntimeError text. Note that ledger.clear() on a source change would erase it too, so keep attempts outside the cleared dictionary.

exercises.title: Choose a real orchestrator
exercises.task: State what framework execution must still qualify.
exercises.check: It includes persistence, scheduling, retries and resource behavior.
exercises.hint: This example is a local mechanism model.
exercises.answer:
Use the existing Prefect route or an explicitly prepared external project to test actual orchestration. Do not call this dictionary a deployed scheduler.

The ledger here lives in memory and vanishes when the process ends, so it cannot survive a worker restart. A real orchestrator must show that the features checkpoint persists across processes and that a retry of publication is detected as already done.

units.diagnosis: If reruns produce duplicated effects, inspect operation identity and publication semantics. If changed inputs reuse old outputs, inspect checkpoint dependencies. If a job outcome is unknown, reconcile it before resubmission. A scheduler's green status does not by itself establish that the correct artifact was published.
units.transfer: Demonstrate a known interruption and an input change, then map those contracts to a real orchestrator with separate persistence and execution evidence.
units.lab: Define checkpoint and retry behavior using artifact identities. Run both complete local examples, explain the changed assumption, and retain evidence for the six practice changes.

units.title: Shadow comparison and stable rollout cohorts
units.outcome: Design stable routing and shadow comparisons with bounded conclusions.
units.theory:
A rollout changes which model participates in a decision. Shadow evaluation can compare predictions without changing user actions. A canary or ramp routes an explicit portion of traffic to a candidate. These mechanisms provide operational evidence, but a prediction difference or a successful router is not automatically evidence of a beneficial causal effect.

Stable assignment is useful when repeated requests from one entity should remain in the same cohort. The first case hashes a declared entity identity into a bounded bucket. Increasing the threshold creates a nested larger cohort. This is a deterministic assignment mechanism, not a guarantee of balance or an analysis of an experiment.

The second case compares scores from two small candidate outputs. Their thresholded decisions agree even though probabilities differ. A single disagreement count would therefore miss a change in confidence. A real rollout policy should consider input compatibility, output behavior, service errors, latency, monitoring and appropriately designed outcome evidence.
key_terms: Shadow evaluation
Scoring requests with a candidate model alongside the active one without changing the action that users receive.
Canary
Routing a small, explicit share of real traffic to a candidate to observe its operational behavior before a wider release.
Stable assignment
Hashing a namespaced entity identity into a fixed bucket so repeated requests from one entity always land in the same cohort.
Ramp
Raising the bucket threshold in steps, which produces nested larger cohorts that keep every earlier member.
Causal evidence
Evidence from an appropriately designed comparison that a change improved outcomes. Score differences or a working router do not provide it.
units.syntax: The hash bucket is computed from a stable namespaced identity and a fixed rule. Keep the rule and salt/version with the rollout contract. Shadow comparison inspects both numeric score changes and derived actions. The fixture's acceptance limit is a declared illustrative threshold, not an estimated business-value rule.

worked.title: Use a stable nested cohort
worked.explanation: The first case assigns one hundred synthetic entities and verifies that a ten-percent bucket range is contained within the twenty-five-percent range. It checks deterministic assignment rather than assuming every small sample has an exact percentage count.
worked.expected: The smaller selected set is a nonempty subset of the larger set, and assignments repeat exactly.

worked.title: Observe score changes without action changes
worked.explanation: The second case has zero decision disagreements at threshold 0.5 but nonzero probability differences. This demonstrates why monitoring only labels can hide a meaningful interface change.
worked.expected: All thresholded decisions agree, while the probabilities have changed.

exercises.title: Change the assignment key
exercises.task: Compare stable customer assignment with per-request random assignment.
exercises.check: The cohort interpretation changes.
exercises.hint: Repeated entities can cross treatments under another rule.
exercises.answer:
Choose the unit from the experiment or rollout design and retain it consistently. Do not assume request-level assignment answers an entity-level question.

With the sha256 rule on f"entity:{i}", the 10 percent ramp selects 8 of 100 entities (0, 27, 35, 43, 60, 77, 89 and 92) and the 25 percent ramp selects 19, and every repeat gives the same sets. Per-request random.random() < 0.10 would put the same customer in both arms across requests, so no customer has a single experience to measure.

exercises.title: Record a salt/version
exercises.task: Add an explicit assignment-version field.
exercises.check: The routing rule is reproducible.
exercises.hint: Hash configuration is part of the decision.
exercises.answer:
Changing it can reassign entities. Treat that as a reviewed change rather than an invisible implementation detail.

Prefixing the key with "v2:" changes the 10 percent cohort to 15 entities, only 2 of which were in the original 8. Recording assignment_version beside each prediction makes that reassignment visible; without it, a jump in the cohort's metrics could be mistaken for a model effect.

exercises.title: Inspect probabilities
exercises.task: Compare score deltas even when decisions agree.
exercises.check: The confidence change remains visible.
exercises.hint: A threshold discards information.
exercises.answer:
Use appropriate numeric and calibration diagnostics alongside action disagreement. A small label difference does not prove equivalent probabilities.

In example_two every probability moves by exactly 0.1, so disagreement is 0 while the first customer's score doubles from 0.1 to 0.2. Reporting only the 0 disagreement would hide that change. Print np.abs(old - candidate) and confirm the maximum is 0.1, under the 0.15 acceptance limit.

exercises.title: Add operational limits
exercises.task: Define acceptable errors and latency for a candidate.
exercises.check: The policy names measured quantities and responses.
exercises.hint: Predictive metrics are not the whole service.
exercises.answer:
Use actual service observations and a rollback rule. The local project supplies bounded HTTP/monitoring checks; production capacity needs separate evidence.

Write limits as quantities the local checker can measure, for example the fraction of 5xx responses and p95 latency over a fixed number of requests, each with the action taken when exceeded. The 0.15 score-delta limit in example_two is a prediction check and says nothing about latency. A limit such as "be careful with errors" cannot fail, so it cannot trigger a pause either.

exercises.title: Avoid a causal claim
exercises.task: Explain what shadow predictions cannot establish about outcomes.
exercises.check: They do not establish the effect of changed actions.
exercises.hint: Users did not receive the candidate action.
exercises.answer:
Use an appropriate randomized or otherwise identified design for that question, with interference, exposure and metric assumptions made explicit.

Shadow scoring never changes an action, so the outcomes observed are those produced by the old model's decisions. Even if the candidate would have offered support to someone, their outcome without the offer is what was recorded.

exercises.title: Plan rollback
exercises.task: Specify the accepted version and state needed if a ramp stops.
exercises.check: A compatible prior bundle is retained.
exercises.hint: Rollback is an operational contract.
exercises.answer:
Restore model and feature compatibility, reconcile in-flight work and record the reason. A pointer switch alone is not every possible recovery requirement.

Keep the previous model, its feature contract and the assignment version together. Rolling back only the model while the 19-entity cohort's feature version remains newer could reintroduce a train/serve mismatch. Test the rollback by scoring the same four rows from example_two after reverting and confirming the old probabilities 0.1, 0.3, 0.6 and 0.9 come back exactly.

units.diagnosis: Unstable cohorts can produce confusing comparisons and repeated exposure changes. Zero disagreement can conceal probability changes. A rollout that meets latency limits can still harm an outcome. Diagnose these separately and connect each decision to the evidence it actually requires.
units.transfer: Separate interface, operational and causal evidence, and retain a compatible rollback target before expanding exposure.
units.lab: Design stable routing and shadow comparisons with bounded conclusions. Run both complete local examples, explain the changed assumption, and retain evidence for the six practice changes.

units.title: Monitoring with delayed labels and bounded service metrics
units.outcome: Monitor operations, data contracts and mature outcomes as distinct signals.
units.theory:
Monitoring observes a running system under incomplete information. Predictions and operational events can arrive immediately, while outcomes may arrive much later. A quality metric computed from whichever labels happen to be available can describe a selected population. Report label maturity and coverage before interpreting the number.

The first case has four predictions but only two mature outcomes at cutoff 5. It computes Brier loss on those two and reports the coverage explicitly. It does not replace the unknown outcomes with negatives. A real analysis should also investigate whether label delay depends on the outcome, entity or intervention.

The second case separates covariate shift from service latency and predictive quality. A large distributional difference is a signal to investigate, not proof that model accuracy changed. A p95 latency from five samples is an observed summary with limited precision, not a service-level guarantee. Monitoring should identify the population, time window, denominator and response for every signal.
key_terms: Monitoring population
The predictions, time window and denominator that a monitoring signal describes, stated before its value is interpreted.
Label coverage
The share of predictions whose outcomes are mature at the monitoring cutoff, here two of four, reported alongside the quality metric.
Selective label availability
Early outcomes can differ systematically from late ones, so a metric on currently available labels may describe a selected population.
Covariate shift
A change in the input distribution, measured here with a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic. It calls for investigation but does not prove lower accuracy.
p95 latency
The 95th percentile of observed response times under an explicit quantile method; five samples give only an imprecise summary.
units.syntax: Filter labels by their availability time, retain prediction identities and calculate coverage against the original prediction population. The example uses an actual two-sample KS statistic for a deliberately separated numeric fixture. Latency uses an explicit quantile method. The real service project keeps only a bounded number of process latency samples and labels that scope in its API.

worked.title: Evaluate only mature observations and retain coverage
worked.explanation: Predictions 1 and 3 have known outcomes by the cutoff. Their squared probability errors average 0.085. The two excluded records remain part of the coverage denominator rather than being discarded from the monitoring story.
worked.expected: Mature-label coverage is 0.5 and observed Brier loss is 0.085.

worked.title: Separate data and operational signals
worked.explanation: The second case shifts every input value by ten and computes a maximal KS statistic on the tiny fixture. It separately reports the chosen latency quantile. Neither signal is described as an observed change in target quality.
worked.expected: The shift statistic is 1.0; the observed higher-method p95 latency is 15 milliseconds.

exercises.title: Move the monitoring cutoff
exercises.task: Advance the cutoff and recompute maturity and coverage.
exercises.check: Newly available labels change the evaluated population.
exercises.hint: Keep the original prediction denominator.
exercises.answer:
Record the cutoff and cohort identities. Comparing different maturity stages without adjustment can create a misleading trend.

At cutoff 5 only predictions 1 and 3 have labels (available at 3 and 5), giving coverage 0.5 and Brier 0.085 from (0.1-0)^2 and (0.6-1)^2. Move the cutoff to 8 and all four labels arrive; prediction 2 (score 0.9, label 1) and prediction 4 (score 0.2, label 0) join. Plotting Brier at cutoff 5 next to Brier at cutoff 8 as if they were two weeks of the same population would be wrong, because the evaluated rows differ.

exercises.title: Test outcome-dependent delay
exercises.task: Describe a process where positive outcomes arrive later.
exercises.check: Early observed quality can be biased.
exercises.hint: Availability may be informative.
exercises.answer:
Investigate delay by outcome and cohort, and use an appropriate evaluation design. Do not assume missing-at-random labels without evidence.

In the fixture the label for prediction 2, the one positive scored 0.9, arrives at time 7, later than both mature rows. If positives systematically arrive late, the early mature set is enriched for negatives and the early Brier describes an easier population. Group label delay by label value and compare.

exercises.title: Interpret drift
exercises.task: Explain what a KS alarm establishes.
exercises.check: It establishes a difference under the tested sample/comparison, not performance loss.
exercises.hint: Input and target behavior are different.
exercises.answer:
Inspect data contracts and evaluate mature outcomes when available. A changed distribution can be harmless, harmful or even beneficial depending on the model and task.

Example_two shifts every baseline value by 10, so the KS statistic is 1.0 with a two-sample p-value near 0.008. That says the distributions differ; it says nothing about Brier, because no label enters the calculation. Treating the alarm as proof of degraded quality would skip the mature-label check.

exercises.title: Record metric scope
exercises.task: State whether a latency summary covers this process or a whole deployment.
exercises.check: The scope is explicit.
exercises.hint: A local counter is not a fleet-wide monitor.
exercises.answer:
Aggregate with suitable identities and windows when designing a real service. Preserve reset/restart behavior in the interpretation.

np.quantile on the five latencies with method="higher" returns 15.0 ms, while the default linear method returns 13.6 ms. State the method, the five-sample window and that the array belongs to one process, otherwise two dashboards can disagree about the same requests.

exercises.title: Choose an action
exercises.task: Define what happens after a freshness or schema alarm.
exercises.check: The response is specific and bounded.
exercises.hint: An alarm without an action is incomplete operations.
exercises.answer:
Use a reviewed reject, fallback, investigation or rollback policy. Avoid silently continuing with invalid inputs while reporting healthy service status.

Name the input, the threshold and the response, for example "reject requests whose region is outside the schema and page the owner". An alert that only increments a counter while /health stays 200 lets invalid inputs keep flowing.

exercises.title: Keep uncertainty visible
exercises.task: Describe the limitations of a quantile from five samples.
exercises.check: The estimate is visibly weak.
exercises.hint: A percentile label does not guarantee precision.
exercises.answer:
Retain counts and distributional context, then collect representative observations for a meaningful service objective or comparison.

With five latencies the 0.95 quantile is essentially the maximum: one slow request moves it from 8 to 15 ms. Report n=5 beside the value so readers see how little evidence stands behind it.

units.diagnosis: A quality improvement can come from changing label coverage. A drift signal can occur without observed performance loss. A latency counter can reset on restart. Inspect populations, windows and evidence types before triggering a broad model replacement.
units.transfer: Keep their denominators and scopes explicit, and connect each to a reviewed response. The real local service demonstrates actual process metrics and stale-feature rejection without claiming production-scale observability.
units.lab: Monitor operations, data contracts and mature outcomes as distinct signals. Run both complete local examples, explain the changed assumption, and retain evidence for the six practice changes.
references: scikit-learn user guide: Metrics and scoring: quantifying the quality of predictions

units.title: Accepted model pointers and rollback after failure
units.outcome: Activate and recover model state through explicit accepted versions.
units.theory:
A candidate model should not become active merely because a file was written. Activation needs accepted artifact identity, interface compatibility and a reviewed decision. Keeping the current pointer separate from candidate files lets a failed candidate leave the accepted model unchanged.

The first case validates a candidate hash before replacing the pointer. A deliberately incorrect expected hash causes rejection while the old pointer bytes remain exact. The second activates a new version and deliberately returns to the prior version. These are local file-state mechanisms, not a distributed transaction across every serving replica.

Atomic visibility and durable recovery are different claims. os.replace gives a useful local replacement boundary, but power-loss durability, remote filesystems, multiple writers and deployment-wide consistency need additional design and qualification. The real Docker project restricts activation to an owned control CLI, validates model structure before publication and keeps the predictor's state mount read-only.
key_terms: Model pointer
A small file naming the accepted active model version and its hash, kept separate from candidate files.
Activation
Replacing the pointer so a candidate becomes active, allowed only after its identity and compatibility checks pass.
Atomic replace
Swapping a fully written pending pointer into place with os.replace, so readers on one local filesystem see the old or new pointer, never a partial one.
Rollback
Pointing back to a prior accepted version, which requires keeping accepted versions available and unchanged.
Durability
Surviving power loss or crashes after a write. It is a separate claim from atomic visibility and needs more than os.replace.
units.syntax: Write a candidate under a versioned name, validate its identity, write a complete pending pointer and replace the current pointer atomically. The pointer records the resolved version and hash. A failed check occurs before the active pointer changes. Preserve accepted versions and define cleanup separately from activation.

worked.title: Reject a bad candidate before activation
worked.explanation: The first case activates v1, records the exact pointer bytes and attempts a v2 activation with a wrong hash. The old pointer must remain unchanged. This tests a specific failure boundary rather than only the successful path.
worked.expected: The failed candidate leaves the active v1 pointer byte-identical.

worked.title: Perform a deliberate rollback
worked.explanation: The second case activates v1, then v2, then v1 again. It checks the final version and absence of a pending pointer. A rollback is recorded as an explicit action, not hidden by deleting candidate evidence.
worked.expected: The accepted version returns to v1 with no pending pointer file.

exercises.title: Validate before switching
exercises.task: List the checks that must precede pointer replacement.
exercises.check: They include artifact identity and compatible structure.
exercises.hint: A valid filename is not enough.
exercises.answer:
The service project also validates feature order, finite coefficients and positive scales. Broader model acceptance still needs its evaluation and operational evidence.

activate() computes sha256 of the written candidate and compares it with expected_hash before writing current.pending. In example_one the hash "0" * 64 cannot match {"weight": 99.0}, so ValueError fires and current.json stays byte-identical to the v1 pointer. Writing the pointer first and validating afterwards would expose consumers to v2 during the gap.

exercises.title: Retain failed evidence
exercises.task: Keep the rejected candidate and its diagnostic in an owned review area.
exercises.check: The failure remains explainable.
exercises.hint: Cleanup is a separate decision.
exercises.answer:
Do not overwrite the previous accepted version or erase the failure merely to simplify directory contents. Apply an explicit retention policy later.

Note that the fixture leaves v2.json on disk after the hash mismatch, because the candidate is written before it is checked. That file is the evidence: record its hash and the ValueError message beside it so a reviewer can see why it was rejected.

exercises.title: Reconcile an unknown response
exercises.task: Describe a timeout after activation may have completed.
exercises.check: The next action reads the pointer before retrying.
exercises.hint: Unknown outcome differs from confirmed rejection.
exercises.answer:
Use the intended version/hash to reconcile actual state. Blindly repeating activation can create misleading audit history in a larger system.

Read current.json and compare its version and sha256 with the intended values. If they already match, the activation completed and the client's timeout lost only the response. Repeating activate() would rewrite the same pointer and add a second audit entry for one change.

exercises.title: Check bundle compatibility
exercises.task: Explain why rolling back only coefficients may be insufficient.
exercises.check: The feature/preprocessing contract must also match.
exercises.hint: Models consume versioned inputs.
exercises.answer:
Restore a compatible model and feature transformation bundle. A file-level rollback can be technically successful while predictions are semantically wrong.

In this fixture the model is a single weight, so the pointer is the whole story. A real bundle also fixes feature order and scaling; restoring v1 coefficients beside a v2 scaler would load cleanly and produce wrong scores.

exercises.title: Separate local and distributed claims
exercises.task: State what os.replace does not establish.
exercises.check: It does not prove multi-replica consensus or power-loss durability.
exercises.hint: One filesystem operation has a limited scope.
exercises.answer:
Use suitable synchronization, persistence and recovery mechanisms for the deployed environment, and test partial failures explicitly.

temporary.replace() maps to os.replace, which is atomic for readers on one local filesystem. It does not fsync the directory, so a power loss could still lose the new pointer, and it coordinates nothing between replicas reading different disks.

exercises.title: Exercise the real project
exercises.task: Use the local-system CLI to activate v2 and return to v1.
exercises.check: Actual HTTP predictions identify the selected version and restore exactly.
exercises.hint: The project is a separate longer-lived workflow.
exercises.answer:
Retain its ownership marker and state. The checker verifies real HTTP, model integrity and replacement without retraining, while leaving external production claims out of scope.

Example_two runs v1, v2, v1 and confirms current.json says v1 with no current.pending left. For the real project, check that HTTP responses report the version and that the v1 hash after rollback equals the original v1 hash.

units.diagnosis: If an invalid candidate becomes active, inspect validation order. If a rollback changes predictions unexpectedly, inspect feature/preprocessing compatibility and artifact identity. If a response is uncertain, reconcile the current version before repeating or cleaning operations.
units.transfer: Test failure before publication and exact rollback behavior, then distinguish local atomicity from the additional guarantees required by a deployed multi-process system.
units.lab: Activate and recover model state through explicit accepted versions. Run both complete local examples, explain the changed assumption, and retain evidence for the six practice changes.

units.title: Model cards, slice evidence and data minimization
units.outcome: Write a model card that is grounded in actual data, metrics and operational decisions.
units.theory:
A model card should make intended use, inputs, evidence, limitations and operational ownership inspectable. It is not a certificate produced by filling a template. A useful card must reflect actual evaluated populations, known failure modes and the decision process used to accept or reject a version.

The first case compares two synthetic slices with different sample sizes and true-positive rates. The counts remain visible, so a rate difference is not presented as a precise population conclusion. One parity metric does not establish fairness, and a model's appropriate use depends on context, harms, alternatives and an adequately designed evaluation.

The second case defines a small input allowlist and rejects an unnecessary email field. Data minimization reduces avoidable exposure and keeps the interface focused on its purpose. It does not establish legal compliance or prove that every allowed feature is appropriate. A real system needs separately qualified governance, access, retention and review processes.
key_terms: Slice metric
A metric such as the true-positive rate computed for one subgroup from its own confusion counts and reported with its denominator.
Sample size
The number of cases behind a slice metric. Small slices give imprecise rates, so a rate difference is not a population conclusion.
Model card
A document recording intended use, inputs, evaluated populations, limitations, owner and rollback version for one model.
Data minimization
Accepting only the fields a purpose needs, enforced here with an input allowlist that rejects an unnecessary email field.
Governance
The access, retention, review and approval processes around a model, which must rest on actual evidence and be qualified separately.
units.syntax: Compute slice metrics from explicit confusion counts and retain their denominators. The card records purpose, permitted features, excluded fields, owner, limits and a rollback version. Compare incoming fields against the allowlist. Keep governance statements tied to actual evidence rather than treating an artifact's filename as approval.

worked.title: Inspect rate differences with counts
worked.explanation: Slice A has twenty observations and true-positive rate 0.8; slice B has ten and rate 0.4. The program reports both counts and rates. Interpretation still requires uncertainty, population and decision context beyond this tiny table.
worked.expected: The two TPRs are 0.8 and 0.4, with different sample sizes.

worked.title: Reject an unnecessary field
worked.explanation: The request includes email even though the declared model interface uses only usage, tickets and region. The program identifies that extra field and retains the card's stated limitations and rollback version.
worked.expected: Email is rejected by the allowlist and the card retains its synthetic-data limit.

exercises.title: Compute a denominator
exercises.task: Identify the denominator of true-positive rate for each slice.
exercises.check: It counts actual positives, not all rows.
exercises.hint: Metric definitions matter.
exercises.answer:
Use tp+fn and retain the underlying counts. Accuracy uses a different denominator and can tell a different story.

Slice A has tp 8 and fn 2, so TPR is 8/10 = 0.8; slice B has tp 2 and fn 3, so TPR is 2/5 = 0.4. Dividing by n (20 and 10) would give 0.4 and 0.2, which are positive counts over all rows rather than recall. Accuracy is 17/20 = 0.85 for A and 6/10 = 0.6 for B. Notice that accuracy and TPR both rank A above B here, but they need not: a slice with many true negatives can have high accuracy and poor recall.

exercises.title: Add uncertainty
exercises.task: Describe an appropriate uncertainty analysis for the slice comparison.
exercises.check: It acknowledges small samples and the sampling/design assumptions.
exercises.hint: A numerical difference is not a complete inference.
exercises.answer:
Use a method appropriate to the cohort and dependence structure, with the original denominators. Avoid a universal fairness conclusion from one noisy metric.

With only 10 and 5 actual positives, 95 percent Wilson intervals are roughly 0.49 to 0.94 for A and 0.12 to 0.77 for B, so they overlap substantially. A bootstrap over rows or an exact interval are reasonable choices, as long as the counts are reported.

exercises.title: Review the purpose
exercises.task: State which decision the model is intended to support.
exercises.check: The intended use is concrete.
exercises.hint: A broad label such as prediction is insufficient.
exercises.answer:
Name the population, action, alternatives and limitations. Changes in intended use require fresh evaluation rather than reusing the same card automatically.

The card names "optional support prioritization": the model ranks who might be offered help. Using the same scores to deny service would be a different decision with different harms and needs its own evaluation. Check the card against each proposed use and record a new review when the action changes.

exercises.title: Minimize inputs
exercises.task: Remove a field with no justified role in the interface.
exercises.check: The accepted schema remains explicit.
exercises.hint: Availability does not justify collection.
exercises.answer:
Review feature necessity and potential harms. Preserve the decision and test rejected fields, rather than accepting arbitrary payloads.

Example_two compares request keys with card["features"] and gets {"email"}. Keep the allowlist in the card and the API schema and test that email is refused; quietly dropping it would hide that clients are sending it.

exercises.title: Record operational ownership
exercises.task: Identify who can accept a model and initiate rollback in a real setting.
exercises.check: The responsibility is acknowledged outside the fixture.
exercises.hint: An owner string is a declaration.
exercises.answer:
Connect it to actual procedures, permissions and retained evidence. Do not describe this synthetic label as an implemented organizational process.

The card says owner "learning team" and rollback_version "v1". In a real setting name the role that may approve activation and the one that may roll back, and where that decision is logged. Writing "learning team" into a production card would imply an on-call rota and approval process that this fixture never implemented.

exercises.title: Bound the claim
exercises.task: Explain why this card is not a compliance certificate.
exercises.check: The answer separates documentation from external requirements and review.
exercises.hint: A template cannot establish every obligation.
exercises.answer:
Use qualified governance processes and appropriate expertise for the real context. Keep this lesson's technical and statistical observations explicit.

The card records purpose, features, limits and a rollback version. Nothing in it shows legal review, consent or regulatory scope, so it supports review but does not replace it. A reader who sees a tidy card might assume approval happened; the field "not_a_legal_compliance_certificate" in example_two exists to block that reading, and the final report should repeat it in prose.

units.diagnosis: A clean aggregate metric can hide a weak slice or a changed population. A long model card can still omit the actual decision and evidence. Avoid converting one rate check, a template or an allowlist into a claim of universal fairness, safety or compliance.
units.transfer: Retain slice denominators, stated limitations and a minimal input contract, and identify which external governance claims require separate review.

units.title: A connected local ML product and real service lifecycle
units.outcome: Deliver a connected local ML product with actual tool execution and a reviewable acceptance decision.
units.theory:
The capstone connects actual components under one information and interface contract. Polars validates and prepares synthetic records. Feast stores feature snapshots and supplies the historical values used for training, then materializes the same feature contract into its SQLite online store. A fitted scikit-learn pipeline predicts from those retrieved fields, MLflow retains its metrics and model card, and a real ASGI request verifies the inference interface.

The training cutoff permits 77 mature labels, while forty later decisions form the declared evaluation cohort. The program independently checks that historical feature retrieval reproduces the expected source values and identifiers. Online inference also checks feature age before use. This makes the feature store an actual part of the computation rather than an unrelated demonstration next to the model.

The ordinary pad remains a bounded fresh-process investigation. The separate complete local-system project adds persistent owned state and a real loopback HTTP server. Its checker covers training, input errors, monitoring, activation/rollback, stale features, corrupted model bytes and predictor replacement without retraining. Those are actual local deployment observations, with external production populations, scale and organizational controls kept separate.
key_terms: Information contract
One shared declaration of fields, clocks and units that Polars preparation, Feast retrieval, training and serving all follow.
Evaluation cohort
The forty later decisions kept apart from the 77 mature-label training rows and used to evaluate the fitted pipeline.
Retrieval check
Confirming that Feast historical features reproduce the expected source values and identifiers before training uses them.
Publication decision
The recorded acceptance or blocking of a model version based on its evidence; the second report explains a deliberately blocked publication.
Loopback service
The separate local-system project's HTTP server on the local machine, whose checker covers activation, rollback, stale features and corrupted model bytes.
units.syntax: Run the complete reference in the data-engineering pad to inspect source-bound JSON reports. The first report records actual training/evaluation, feature-store and inference evidence; the second explains a deliberately blocked publication decision. For the longer-lived workflow, copy projects/local-system to an owned work directory and use its README/run.sh. Its state is separate from the classroom's saved code and notes.

worked.title: Connect the actual data and model boundaries
worked.explanation: The first case retrieves all 120 historical decisions through Feast, fits on 77 eligible rows, evaluates 40 later rows, materializes online features and submits an in-process HTTP request. MLflow readback checks the recorded metric, and the classroom report retains the contract and outcome.
worked.expected: All 120 requests reconcile, model input/output is valid, and the report identifies actual local tools and the no-external-deployment boundary.

worked.title: Block a candidate with inadequate evidence
worked.explanation: The second case has valid schema and artifact identity but only 0.1 mature-label coverage against a required 0.8. Publication is rejected and the accepted version remains v1. This demonstrates that structural success alone is insufficient.
worked.expected: The publication decision is false with an explicit coverage reason and retained accepted version.

exercises.title: Trace the training features
exercises.task: Identify where the actual training values came from.
exercises.check: They came through the registered Feast historical retrieval.
exercises.hint: Follow identifiers and time boundaries.
exercises.answer: Compare them with the independent prepared source and verify complete request coverage. A separate successful store demo would not prove this connection.

exercises.title: Review label maturity
exercises.task: Explain why only 77 rows enter fitting.
exercises.check: The training cutoff excludes labels not yet known.
exercises.hint: The retrospective table contains future outcomes.
exercises.answer: Preserve the cutoff and included identities. Do not select training rows merely because their prediction times are earlier.

exercises.title: Inspect the saved report
exercises.task: Read the feature contract, age, metric and source identity.
exercises.check: Each claim has a defined local scope.
exercises.hint: A report should be evidence, not a success slogan.
exercises.answer: Verify actual readback and distinguish package execution, numerical assertions, evaluation interpretation and deployment qualification.

exercises.title: Run the real local service
exercises.task: Use the copied project and its Docker-only instructions.
exercises.check: The loopback HTTP endpoint predicts from durable owned state.
exercises.hint: The pad itself does not keep a server alive.
exercises.answer: The project has explicit training, serving and control roles. Its checker proves declared local lifecycle behavior and cleans only its owned resources.

exercises.title: Exercise rollback and stale inputs
exercises.task: Activate the candidate, restorev 1 and test stale-feature rejection in the project.
exercises.check: Versioned predictions and diagnostics follow the contract.
exercises.hint: Do not change timestamps merely to hide stale data.
exercises.answer: Retain accepted artifacts, preserve true feature age and record the operational decision. Monitoring and publication are part of the product.

exercises.title: Write the final acceptance argument
exercises.task: State what supports release and what remains external.
exercises.check: It separates local evidence from broader deployment claims.
exercises.hint: Every assertion has a scope.
exercises.answer: Cite the data/interface contracts, actual tool results, diagnostics, persistent state and rollback checks. Identify additional scale, security, population and governance qualification required for a real use.

units.diagnosis: If any boundary fails, diagnose the earliest mismatched contract rather than relabeling the whole pipeline successful. Check request coverage, clocks, feature identity, preprocessing, model version, artifact bytes and actual service responses. Keep candidate output separate from accepted publication and preserve meaningful failure evidence.
units.transfer: Use the owned service project to test persistent HTTP operation and recovery, then specify the additional evidence needed before adapting the design to a real organization and population.
units.lab: Deliver a connected local ML product with actual tool execution and a reviewable acceptance decision. Run both complete local examples, explain the changed assumption, and retain evidence for the six practice changes.

project_summary: The owned local-system project adds a real loopback HTTP prediction service with explicit Docker training, persistent local Feast/MLflow/model state, monitoring, controlled activation and rollback. Its lifecycle is separate from the bounded classroom pad; copy and operate it through the documented owner-aware launcher.
